title: Song 5:1 — the Greek has a clause before “I am come into my garden” that the KJV and Hebrew lack
summary: The KJV verse begins “I am come into my garden”. Brenton’s Greek prints a sentence before it: let my kinsman come down into his garden and eat his fruit.
text: KJV Song of Solomon 5:1: “I am come into my garden, my sister, my spouse: I have gathered my myrrh with my spice; I have eaten my honeycomb with my honey; I have drunk my wine with my milk: eat, O friends; drink, yea, drink abundantly, O beloved.” Hebrew (WLC) 5:1: בָּ֣אתִי לְגַנִּי֮ אֲחֹתִ֣י כַלָּה֒ אָרִ֤יתִי מֹורִי֙ עִם־בְּשָׂמִ֔י אָכַ֤לְתִּי יַעְרִי֙ עִם־דִּבְשִׁ֔י שָׁתִ֥יתִי יֵינִ֖י עִם־חֲלָבִ֑י אִכְל֣וּ רֵעִ֔ים שְׁת֥וּ וְשִׁכְר֖וּ דֹּודִֽים׃ Brenton’s Greek 5:1: Καταβήτω ἀδελφιδός μου εἰς κῆπον αὐτοῦ, καὶ φαγέτω καρπὸν ἀκροδρύων αὐτοῦ· εἰσῆλθον εἰς κῆπόν μου ἀδελφή μου νύμφη· ἐτρύγησα σμύρναν μου μετὰ ἀρωμάτων μου, ἔφαγον ἄρτον μου μετὰ μέλιτός μου, ἔπιον οἶνόν μου μετὰ γάλακτός μου· φάγετε πλήσιοι καὶ πίετε, καὶ μεθύσθητε ἀδελφοί. Brenton’s own English (https://ebible.org/eng-Brenton/SNG05.htm) prints: “Let my kinsman come down into his garden, and eat the fruit of his choice berries. I am come into my garden, my sister, my spouse: I have gathered my myrrh with my spices; I have eaten my bread with my honey; I have drunk my wine with my milk. Eat, O friends, and drink; yea, brethren, drink abundantly.”. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/22/5/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/SNG05.htm.
reasoning: The Hebrew verse opens with בָּאתִי לְגַנִּי (“I have come to my garden”). The Greek verse has two sentences before that point is reached: Καταβήτω ἀδελφιδός μου εἰς κῆπον αὐτοῦ, καὶ φαγέτω καρπὸν ἀκροδρύων αὐτοῦ. The KJV therefore has one speaker arriving in the garden; the Greek page first prints an invitation, in the third person, for the beloved to come down to ‘his’ garden and eat its fruit, then the arrival. The KJV and Hebrew have no such opening clause.
scope: T applies to the clause quoted only. The verse is also not word for word the same at the end (the KJV has “honeycomb”, the Greek ἄρτον, ‘bread’); only the added opening clause is compared here. This compares the wording of three texts. It does not show which wording is original, and it does not say what the Hebrew word means beyond the words quoted. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew manuscripts were not examined. The Greek quoted is Brenton's printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient Greek translation tradition of the Old Testament. title: Song 5:8 — “I charge you” in the KJV; the Greek adds “by the powers and by the forces of the field”
summary: In the KJV the woman charges the daughters of Jerusalem to tell him she is sick of love. In Brenton’s Greek the charge is sworn by the powers and the forces of the field.
text: KJV Song of Solomon 5:8: “I charge you, O daughters of Jerusalem, if ye find my beloved, that ye tell him, that I am sick of love.” Hebrew (WLC) 5:8: הִשְׁבַּ֥עְתִּי אֶתְכֶ֖ם בְּנֹ֣ות יְרוּשָׁלִָ֑ם אִֽם־תִּמְצְאוּ֙ אֶת־דֹּודִ֔י מַה־תַּגִּ֣ידוּ לֹ֔ו שֶׁחֹולַ֥ת אַהֲבָ֖ה אָֽנִי׃ Brenton’s Greek 5:8: Ὥρκισα ὑμᾶς θυγατέρες Ἱερουσαλὴμ ἐν ταῖς δυνάμεσι καὶ ἐν ταῖς ἰσχύσεσι τοῦ ἀγροῦ· ἐὰν εὕρητε τὸν ἀδελφιδόν μου, τί ἀπαγγείλητε αὐτῷ; ὅτι τετρωμένη ἀγάπης ἐγώ εἰμι. Brenton’s own English (https://ebible.org/eng-Brenton/SNG05.htm) prints: “I have charged you, O daughters of Jerusalem, by the powers and the virtues of the field: if ye should find my kinsman, what are ye to say to him? That I am wounded with love.”. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/22/5/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/SNG05.htm.
reasoning: The Hebrew has הִשְׁבַּעְתִּי אֶתְכֶם בְּנוֹת יְרוּשָׁלִַם and goes straight to אִם־תִּמְצְאוּ. The Greek, after Ὥρκισα ὑμᾶς θυγατέρες Ἱερουσαλήμ, adds ἐν ταῖς δυνάμεσι καὶ ἐν ταῖς ἰσχύσεσι τοῦ ἀγροῦ (Brenton’s English: “by the powers and the virtues of the field”). The KJV charge names nothing it is sworn by; the Greek names two. The KJV also has the women told the message as a clause, the Greek as a question, τί ἀπαγγείλητε αὐτῷ; (“what are ye to say to him?”); that second contrast is not compared here.
scope: T applies to the clause quoted only. Only the added oath phrase is compared. The KJV “sick” and Brenton’s “wounded” are different English words for the same clause; this record does not rest on them, and the Hebrew word is not defined here. This compares the wording of three texts. It does not show which wording is original, and it does not say what the Hebrew word means beyond the words quoted. title: Song 8:2 — the KJV has “who would instruct me”; the Greek has “the chamber of her that conceived me”
summary: The KJV brings him to her mother’s house, “who would instruct me”. Brenton’s Greek brings him to the house and into the chamber of the woman who conceived her, and prints no ‘instruct’.
text: KJV Song of Solomon 8:2: “I would lead thee, and bring thee into my mother’s house, who would instruct me: I would cause thee to drink of spiced wine of the juice of my pomegranate.” Hebrew (WLC) 8:2: אֶנְהָֽגֲךָ֗ אֲבִֽיאֲךָ֛ אֶל־בֵּ֥ית אִמִּ֖י תְּלַמְּדֵ֑נִי אַשְׁקְךָ֙ מִיַּ֣יִן הָרֶ֔קַח מֵעֲסִ֖יס רִמֹּנִֽי׃ Brenton’s Greek 8:2: Παραλήψομαί σε, εἰσάξω σε εἰς οἶκον μητρός μου καὶ εἰς ταμεῖον τῆς συλλαβούσης με· ποτιῶ σε ἀπὸ οἴνου τοῦ μυρεψικοῦ, ἀπὸ νάματος ῥοῶν μου. Brenton’s own English (https://ebible.org/eng-Brenton/SNG08.htm) prints: “I would take thee, I would bring thee into my mother's house, and into the chamber of her that conceived me; I would make thee to drink of spiced wine, of the juice of my pomegranates.”. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/22/8/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/SNG08.htm.
reasoning: The Hebrew has אֶל־בֵּית אִמִּי תְּלַמְּדֵנִי, where the last word is the verb the KJV renders “who would instruct me”. The Greek prints εἰς οἶκον μητρός μου καὶ εἰς ταμεῖον τῆς συλλαβούσης με, adding a second place, ταμεῖον (‘chamber’), and no word that Brenton renders ‘instruct’. The KJV’s mother teaches; the Greek’s house has a chamber.
scope: T applies to the clause quoted only. KJV “my mother’s house, who would instruct me” is one reading of the Hebrew clause; this record does not say the Hebrew cannot be read otherwise and does not define the Hebrew verb. title: Song 8:4 — the KJV charge is unsworn; the Greek adds “by the forces of the field”
summary: The KJV charges the daughters of Jerusalem not to stir up love. Brenton’s Greek swears the charge “by the virtues of the field”.
text: KJV Song of Solomon 8:4: “I charge you, O daughters of Jerusalem, that ye stir not up, nor awake my love, until he please.” Hebrew (WLC) 8:4: הִשְׁבַּ֥עְתִּי אֶתְכֶ֖ם בְּנֹ֣ות יְרוּשָׁלִָ֑ם מַה־תָּעִ֧ירוּ ׀ וּֽמַה־תְּעֹֽרְר֛וּ אֶת־הָאַהֲבָ֖ה עַ֥ד שֶׁתֶּחְפָּֽץ׃ Brenton’s Greek 8:4: Ὥρκισα ὑμᾶς θυγατέρες Ἱερουσαλὴμ ἐν ταῖς ἰσχύσεσι τοῦ ἀγροῦ· ἐὰν ἐγείρητε καὶ ἐὰν ἐξεγείρητε τὴν ἀγάπην ἕως ἂν θελήσῃ. Brenton’s own English (https://ebible.org/eng-Brenton/SNG08.htm) prints: “I have charged you, ye daughters of Jerusalem, by the virtues of the field, that ye stir not up, nor awake my love, until he please.”. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/22/8/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/SNG08.htm.
reasoning: The Hebrew of this verse reads הִשְׁבַּעְתִּי אֶתְכֶם בְּנוֹת יְרוּשָׁלִַם and then מַה־תָּעִירוּ; nothing in it follows the address to the daughters but the charge itself. The Greek puts ἐν ταῖς ἰσχύσεσι τοῦ ἀγροῦ after the address. This is the same added phrase as at 5:8, and appears in this verse in the Greek only.
scope: T applies to the clause quoted only. The Hebrew of other verses (the Song’s earlier charges) is not compared here; the record is limited to the wording of 8:4 in the three texts quoted. This compares the wording of three texts. It does not show which wording is original, and it does not say what the Hebrew word means beyond the words quoted. title: Song 8:5 — “from the wilderness” in the KJV; the Greek has her “all white”
summary: The KJV asks who is coming up from the wilderness leaning on her beloved. Brenton’s Greek asks who is coming up made white, and prints no wilderness.
text: KJV Song of Solomon 8:5: “Who is this that cometh up from the wilderness, leaning upon her beloved? I raised thee up under the apple tree: there thy mother brought thee forth: there she brought thee forth that bare thee.” Hebrew (WLC) 8:5: מִ֣י זֹ֗את עֹלָה֙ מִן־הַמִּדְבָּ֔ר מִתְרַפֶּ֖קֶת עַל־דֹּודָ֑הּ תַּ֤חַת הַתַּפּ֙וּחַ֙ עֹֽורַרְתִּ֔יךָ מָּה חִבְּלַ֣תְךָ אִמֶּ֔ךָ שָׁ֖מָּה חִבְּלָ֥ה יְלָדַֽתְךָ׃ Brenton’s Greek 8:5: Τίς αὕτη ἡ ἀναβαίνουσα λελευκανθισμένη, ἐπιστηριζομένη ἐπὶ τὸν ἀδελφιδὸν αὐτῆς; Ὑπὸ μῆλον ἐξήγειρά σε· ἐκεῖ ὠδίνησέ σε ἡ μήτηρ σου, ἐκεῖ ὠδίνησέ σε ἡ τεκοῦσά σε. Brenton’s own English (https://ebible.org/eng-Brenton/SNG08.htm) prints: “Who is this that comes up all white, leaning on her kinsman? I raised thee up under an apple-tree; there thy mother brought thee forth; there she that bore thee brought thee forth.”. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/22/8/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/SNG08.htm.
reasoning: The Hebrew has מִן־הַמִּדְבָּר (“from the wilderness”). The Greek verse prints ἡ ἀναβαίνουσα λελευκανθισμένη, where the participle is the word Brenton gives as ‘all white’; no word for the wilderness appears in this edition’s verse. The KJV’s question is about where she comes from; the Greek’s is about how she looks.
scope: T applies to the clause quoted only. Brenton’s edition only: other editions of the Greek may print “from the wilderness” (ἀπὸ τῆς ἐρήμου). That has not been checked here, so the record is a comparison of the Hebrew with this one printed edition. This compares the wording of three texts.
